newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-US current account to fall victim of dlr.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-US current account to fall victim of dlr.

text.p: U.S. current account estimates in the latest Reuters quarterly survey called for a sharper deterioration in the 1997 and 1998 deficit than expected in last quarter's poll due to U.S. outperformance of overseas economies and the dollar's inspired rise.
"We've got a strong U.S. economy and a weak foreign economy. That's going to hurt us," said David Wyss, research director at DRI/McGraw Hill.
"The biggest impact is going to come from the dollar," said Tim O'Neill, chief economist at Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal.

"Even though the real cycle adjustments would lead you to expect an improving trade balance coming out of slowing growth in the U.S. and strengthening growth overseas, at least for the time being, that effect will be overwhelmed by the lag impact of a stronger dollar," O'Neill said.
Significant long-term changes in foreign exchange rates usually experience a lag of one to two years before impacting exports and imports -- a well-accepted economic theory known as the J-curve.
On average, the 12 economists polled in April forecast a $185.0 billion shortfall in 1997 compared to a $176.3 billion deficit predicted in the January 29 survey.
For 1998, the deficit forecasts grew to a $192.7 billion shortfall from a previously forecast $175.8 billion gap.
These latest survey results reversed the year-to-year trend to a worsening, rather than improving, trade gap.

Economists said the recent strength of the dollar, which hit a three-year high at 1.7375 marks last week and a 56-month peak of 127.16 yen on April 10, would overpower any eventual impact from a U.S. economic slowdown and pick-up overseas.

In the short-run, a change in exchange rates can even have the opposite effect on trade than would be expected. So a rising dollar could temporarily encourage exports and discourage imports, thus reducing the trade gap.
"It's not too much a dollar issue this year. Because of the J-curve, a stronger dollar actually helps you in the short-run," Wyss said.
The dollar has made a significant recovery since it fell to its post-WWII lows of 1.3438 marks and 79.75 yen in March and April of 1995, respectively.
Analysts said they revised their forecasts as a more prolonged divergence between the U.S. and overseas economies became apparent in recent months.

"We will probably see a bit of improvement next year overseas, but it is still not clear they will catch up to the United States. Japan looks awfully sluggish and Europe is too busy shooting itself in the foot trying to set up (European Monetary Union)," Wyss said.

On a quarterly basis, the mean forecast showed a steady widening from the second-quarter 1997 deficit of $45.3 billion until a brief leveling out in the last two quarters of 1998 at roughly a $47.1 billion shortfall.
However, the deficit should widen to $50.9 billion in the first quarter of 1999, the survey showed.
